units.translation: 1295. 〈ἄκμηνοι:〉 unspeakable. And Nicander (Ther. 116): ‘ἄκμηνοι σίτων’. Sᵐ
1297. The order is: they were lamenting by the daughter of Aeetes.
1299a. χηραμοῦ: of a hiding-place. Lᴳ (P)
b. ἀπτήνες: those unable to fly.
1300. Pactolus is a river of Lydia, now called Chrysorrhoas.
1304. ἰήλεμον: instead of θρῆνον; it is derived from Ialemus, the son of the Muse.
1305. ἐλίασθεν: instead of they died. Lᴳ P
1306. 〈δαῆναι:〉 to be known. Gᴳ

1309a. ἡρώισσαι: Herodian in the eleventh book (I 270, 31 L.) says, with a circumflex on the penult, from the contraction of ἡρώισσαι — for the feminine of ἥρως becomes ἡρώισσα — [or] instead of ἡρωῖναι. τιμήοροι are the guardians of Libya or those honored in Libya [heroines].
b. τιμήοροι: avengers. Lᴳ Gᴳ Sᵐ P
1310. ἦμος ὅτ’ ἐκ πα〈τρός〉: Stesichorus (fg 62 B. III 226) was the first to say that Athena leapt with her weapons from the head of Zeus.

1311. Triton is a river of Libya, and there is also one in Boeotia. Athena is thought to have been born by one of them, from which she is also called Tritogeneia. So some say; but others: or from τρεῖν, which means to frighten, because she instills fear in her enemies.
1312. θέρον: they were warming, burning. Lᴳ P
1314. πέπλον: properly the woman's garment. Lᴳ (P)
1315. παλιμπετές: falling back, backwards. Lᴳ Gᴳ (P)
1317. ἀτυζόμενον: ἀτύζω; from ἄτη comes the verb ἀτῶ, from which is derived ἀτύω, as from ὀλῶ comes ὀλύω and ὀλλύω, and with the addition of ζ, ἀτύζω, just as from ἀτίω comes ἀτίζω.
1318. ἀμηχανίῃ: helplessness. Lᴳ (P)

1322. οἰοπόλοι: those who tend sheep, and they are the Epimelides. He called them chthonian because they are daughters of Libya. Or chthonian means earth-born, and with human voice because they come to speak with men.
Callimachus mentions the Nymphs, speaking thus (fg 126 Schn.): ‘Mistresses of Libya, heroines, who watch over the fold of the Nasamones and the long sandbanks, increase my mother while she lives.’
1327-28. σφετέρῃ: he should have said ὑμετέρᾳ. He speaks to the ship; for it carries them in its hull as a mother in her womb.

1329. Ἀχαιίδα: by Achaeis he means either Thessaly or Greece. Better Thessaly; for its inhabitants are called Achaeans. Homer (B 681): ‘now those who dwelt in Pelasgian Argos,’ then (684): ‘they were called Myrmidons and Hellenes and Achaeans.’ L
1333. ἵλατ’ ἐρημονόμοι: be gracious, you who dwell in the desert.
1339. ὠρύεται: instead of cries out; it is the sound of lions.
1342. βουπελάται: the cowherds. It is said either with the π being redundant — for they are βουελάται — or from being near the cattle, which is better.
1348. στέρφεσι: with hides; hence στερφιῶσαι. Ibycus (fg 59 B. III 252) called an army στερφωτῆρα, meaning one that has hides.
